This observation combines data from 2 Inaturalist observations, each from a distinct owl pellet; the 2 pellets were found 2 feet apart. The second pellet was found 2 days later (I probably missed the first time).

What is remarkable is that  separate owl pellets contain bones that  seem to be from the same prey (a rabbit).

The rabbit left femur found in pellet #2 matches perfectly the rabbit pelvis found in pellet #1. More precisely, the femur head (convex part of the hip joint) fits perfectly in the acetabulum (concave part of the joint) of the pelvis. found in pellet #1

It is very likely that the 2 separate pellets contain the bones of the same rabbit. However, we cannot affirm that they come from the same owl. We know there is a mated pair of great horned owls in this area; they could have shared the same prey.

Scientific & Common Name:

The Scientific name for the organism of interest is Sylvilagus floridanus which is commonly known as Eastern Cottontail Rabbit. 

Habitat & Geographic Range: 
 
	According to the Wildlife Habitat Management Institute (1999), eastern cottontail extends from southern Canada to Central America and mainly found in eastern two-thirds of the United States excluding Maine, most regions in New Hampshire and Vermont as well as northeastern New York.  The eastern cottontail existence is an effect due to the introduction of the species by the state and private agencies in the beginning of the twenty -first century. The species lives and thrives in dense forest especially clearings and edges of these forests. Also, common residence include meadows, farmlands, brushy fields and residential spaces. In certain situations, hollow logs or unoccupied burrows of another animal will shelter the cottontail as it does not dig their own burrows (Saunders, 1988).

Size / Weight & Lifespan: 

	The approximate length range of the an adult eastern cottontail is 380-461 mm and weight the is around 1.8-3.0 lb., the female is usually slightly larger than the male rabbit. One way the organism is distinguishable from a snowshoe hare is its smaller size and the lack of white winter coat (Saunders, 1988).  In the wild, the average lifespan of an eastern cottontail is less than three years; however, the cottontail rabbit can live up to eight years (Lee, 2000).

Diet:
	
       Based on the article from Wildlife Habitat Management Institute (1999), the eastern cottontail’s diet is a broad range of different variety of foods depending on the available supply in the environment which is mainly green vegetation, woody plants and fruits. For example, orchard grass, redtop, bluegrasses, wheat-grasses, common lawn grasses, wild strawberry, blackberry, raspberry, dandelion, green beans, peas, cabbage, maple, willow, corn, and soybean. The foods regularly consumed by the organism contain sufficient amount of water for daily hydration (Wildlife Habitat Management Institute, 1999). 

Reproduction & Communication: 

	The breeding season is from February or March till September which females produce litters during this time, usually 4-5. The gestation time period is approximately 28-30 days which varies with the number of litters produced. The female will prepare a shallow depression in the soil and lines it will her own fur a few days before birth of the litters. The newborn litters are blind in the first week and weigh 25-28 g. The mother visits her litters at dawn and at dusk to nurser them before leaving and protecting them from potential predators. When the young reaches 16 days of age, the young will begin to forge for vegetation nearby the nest. The mother continues to nurse her young before they separate and the young becomes independent. The young cottontail might breed in the following summer since its birth in the same year during the spring but many become sexual mature a year later.  Eastern cottontails convey multi-sensory cues in their social interactions consisting of visual, chemical, tactile and vocal signals.  For example, the adult cottontail will hit with their hind feet rapidly on the ground to convey an alarm signal. Cottontails give a high pitched scream when distressed, injured  or captured by a predator. In the instance of male and female sexual interaction, the two will engage in a ritualized motor pattern behaviour of male chasing the female as they run and leap toward each other as the male tries to urinate on her to display interest ( Saunders, 1988).

Predation: 

	Many carnivorous animals consider the eastern cottontail as an essential part of their diet. Some of the main predators are Red-tails hawks, great horned owls, foxes, coyotes, weasels, bobcats and minks (Saunders, 1988).

Conservation Status:

	Herbivores such as eastern cottontail rabbits cause sequential damage on vegetation in urban gardens and green lands in North America which cost the wildlife damage approximately 3 billion dollars per year. European rabbits were introduced into Europe as invasive species as well as Australia which have caused soil erosion, damage to crops and risked the survivorship of native species. As a result of the consequences, Australia contributes to rabbit population control using poison baiting, immunocontraception and introduced diseases. Similarly, eastern cottontail rabbit demonstrate the exact issue in North America. The cottontail rabbit migrate to urban parks during the winter which they damage vegetation of that region ( Hunt et al., 2013).  Despite the eastern cottontails being a prominent game species, they are common throughout their range and are not endangered species ( Mikita, 1999).

1. Scientific name: Sylvilagus floridanus
Common name: Eastern cottontail rabbit

2. Habitat & Geographic Range
The Sylvilagus floridanus, commonly known as the eastern cottontail rabbit, is found across the Americas, including Colombia and Venezuela.1 Spread across a diverse range of locations, historically amongst swamps and prairies, the eastern cottontail is adept at surviving among clearings, fields, and large open areas.2 A common requirement in the eastern cottontail's habitat is the use of shrubbery, which allows them to hide from predators and seek cover from the environment and weather.1 While not commonly found in densely wooded locations, the eastern cottontail may also be found along the fringes of forests and urban habitats.2 More recently, and perhaps due to human involvement, the eastern cottontail has also been found to thrive in farmland and pastures closer to urbanization.2

3. Size/Weight & Lifespan
The size and weight of the eastern cottontail ranges from approximately 15.5 to 18.75 inches and 28 to 54 ounces.3 As this species inhabits a diverse range of locations, geographic variation also plays a role in its range of body sizes. In a study in 2000 examining 3 regions of cottontail inhabitation, researchers analyzed cranial and mandibular measurements from museum collections within each region to identify trends.4 Adult measurements were used to prevent age-related variables, and researchers concluded from the morphological trends relating body size and geographic parameters that body size decreased from east to west within the range.4 This study was the most recent work on the correlation between geographic location and body size within conducted research. Environmental factors are also known to affect life span and rate of growth in the eastern cottontail. In the wild, this species may live up to 3 years depending on predation, resource availability, and other factors.3

4. Diet
The diet of the eastern cottontail is seasonally dependent, as this species will adapt to the available resources of its habitat. While in the spring, the open field areas provide grass and herbs to graze on, if they are located closer to urban areas, they will also feed on garden fare like lettuce and home-grown vegetation.3 In the fall and winter seasons, when the resources are scarcer, their diets consist of more woody species such as bark and twigs.3 

5. Reproduction & Communication
The onset of reproductive maturity for eastern cottontail females occurs around 2-3 months of age.5 Their mating system is not only polygynous, but females are polyestrous and typically breed 3-4 times a year.5 As studies of the reproduction of the cottontail were conducted in the past lacking significant recent discoveries, the majority of known information comes from observational studies published in 1963.5 A small population of individually marked cottontails were placed into a field enclosure and their behaviour was observed, allowing researchers to detail their reproductive behaviour.5 As a result, interactions between mating cottontails have been seen to include the mating ritual, which involves the male chasing the female until she turns and spars with her forepaws, then a series of leaps will occur until the pair mates.5 Breeding conditions vary; however, as average breeding occurs from February to September.6 When giving birth, the females dig shallow, lined nests and provide minimal care for the young, which leave around 7 weeks after birth.5

The eastern cottontail mainly communicates through a series of vocalizations, ranging from distress cries, squeals during copulation, and grunts.5 Distress cries are typically used to startle predators and warn others of incoming danger, as despite being mostly solitary mammals, they maintain a sense of community.7 Grunts are also used in a similar manner when predators approach nesting females.7 Chemical communication through pheromones is also used to a lesser degree within this species. As cottontails possess 100 million sensory receptors in their nose, twitching allows for these chemoreceptors to be exposed.7 Pheromones are typically present in the mate-selection process.7 The eastern cottontail rabbit is also crepuscular and nocturnal, so most communication occurs when they are active in the night.7

6. Predation 
While the population of cottontails is increasing, predation of this species is being affected by both wildlife and human interference. Through a series of study sites in Massachusetts, predators of the eastern cottontail have been observed over a 2-year period to include coyotes, red foxes, great horned owls, and red-tailed hawks.8 When escaping predation, cottontails exhibit behaviour such as freezing or flushing, which consists of escaping by rapid zig-zagging bounds.8 In terms of human impact, the encroachment on previously available habitats have caused the cottontail population to move into increasingly urban and suburban areas.9 Human hunters have also been a persistent predator of the cottontail, as these rabbits are a popular game animal for their meat, fur, and sport.8 While research into the effects of hunting have recently shown little impact on the population of cottontails along the Cape Cod National Seashore, closer examination for future impacts will be useful. 

7. Conservation Status
The eastern cottontail rabbit is termed the Least Concern for its conservation status.10

8. Did You Know?
The eastern cottontail rabbit can reach speeds of up to 18 miles/hour, almost 30 km/hour!8

Scientific & Common Name(s)

Scientific Name: Genus Syvilagus
Common Name: Eastern Cottontail Rabbits


Habitat & Geographic Range:

 	The Cottontail rabbits are a genus that is widely distributed, spreading  throughout the northern half of South America, as well as North and Central America. Habitats range from Southern Canada to Northern South America, with some species within the genus dispersing themselves further than others. The habitats occupied by the Cottontail rabbits vary in diversity, seeing as there are many optimal locations available to satisfy their habitat requirements (In Chapman, In Flux, & International Union for Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources, 1990, p. 95).  Favorable habitat traits include an abundance of coverage for escape, such as a sage bush (Artemesia sp.), bramble (Rubus sp.) or Frailejones (Espeletia sp.), and is often characterized by perennial grasses and forbs. 


Size /Weight & Lifespan:

 	The Eastern Cottontail rabbits begin their life born into a nest as a litter. They vary in terms of size with the largest member of the genus being the Swamp Cottontail, at approximately 2,000g, and the smallest member being the Pygmy Cottontail, at approximately 400g. The females in the Syvilagus genus can range from being 1 to 10% larger than their male counterparts. All Cottontails, however, possess rather large feet and ears in comparison to their bodies. The lifespan of an Eastern Cottontail raised in the wild is approximately less than 3 years, however within captivity they are able to reach 8 years. 


Diet:

 	Most Eastern Cottontails have two main dietary periods, with one extending from October up until May, called the winter period (Green & Flinders, 1991, p. 63). The summer period refers to the rest of the months remaining (from June-September). From the food items consumed, many are taken in at relatively similar amounts such as forbs, grasses and shrubs. Amongst the different habitat sites, there were not many variations in regards to their feeding habits, however preferences appear in terms of eating certain foods during a specific dietary period. The Sagebush for example was eaten very highly within the winter compared to other foods. However, it was also one food item that was eaten nearly year round, never having a relative frequency less then 36% within the cottontail’s scat. This is in comparison to the summer period, where popular food items include grass (such as wheatgrass and Nevada bluegrass) as well as forbs (Green & Flinders, 1991, p. 63).


Reproduction & Communication:

 	 Cottontail rabbits reproduce at extremely high rates and reach sexual maturity within one year. The mating ritual normally occurs after dark, with the female turning towards the male after a chase. They face each other crouching until one member jumps up about 2 feet into the air. This behaviour is repeated by both sexes until mating begins. The mating sound heard is a soft squealing noise. The breeding season length of the Cottontails is dependent on the rabbit’s location, ranging from 7-9 months; often starting from December-January. The litter size often produced by this genus is 2.6-3.6 young per litter, depicting small sizes (Orr 1940, Sowls 1957, Chapman and Morgan 1974). 


Predation: Does the animal have any predators?

 	The list of predators of the cottontail rabbits is extraneous. In regards to the young, their main predators include American crows as well as shrikes. Predators that prey on both adults as well as the young, however include the great-horned owl and red-tailed hawks. Other main predators include red squirrels, dogs, foxes and when present weasels (Hanrahan, 2012). The biggest threat to the Cottontails is unsurprisingly, humans, which cause a numerous amount of Cottontail rabbit deaths annually through hunting as well as car accidents. If found by a predator, these rabbits often run extremely fast in a zig-zag pattern in order to lose their pursuer. It’s first response to a predator’s presence, however, is to freeze so as to attempt to go by unnoticed. (Hanrahan, 2012).


Conservation Status:

 	Within the U.S., the eastern cottontail was considered a candidate species for the Endangered Species Act (ESA) from 2006-2015. However, in response to huge conservation efforts completed, they no longer fit the description of being threatened or endangered. Resulting in their removal from the list of candidate species (Scanlon, 2013).


Did You Know?

 	Did you know that Eastern Cottontail rabbits are animals that are almost completely mute? Other than screeching or screaming quite loudly if caught by predators, they communicate predominantly through thumping their back feet against the ground. (Hamilton, 1940, p. 9).

Desert Cottontails and Brush Rabbits look similar at a distance, but when you focus on their body shape, coloring, and behavior, they separate into two very different species. Desert cottontails have noticeably longer ears that end in a dark tip, and these ears stand out even when the rabbit is resting. Their fur shows warm, rusty tones along the back of the neck and on the hindlegs, giving them a slightly sun‑washed look. The tail is rounded and fluffy with a bright white edge that flashes clearly when the animal runs, which makes them easy to spot as they bound across open ground. Brush rabbits, on the other hand, have shorter ears that stay a uniform gray with no dark tip. Their coat is a cool slate‑gray without any rufous highlights, and their tail is smaller and more muted, blending into the rest of the body rather than standing out. These differences are subtle, but once you learn them, they are reliable ways to tell the two species apart.
Their habitats reflect these physical differences. Desert cottontails are widespread across the southwestern United States and northern Mexico, thriving in open or lightly vegetated areas such as desert grasslands, chaparral, pinyon‑juniper woodlands, and the edges of riparian corridors. They often rest in shallow depressions or take over abandoned burrows from other mammals, especially during the heat of the day. Brush rabbits have a much narrower range, hugging the Pacific coast from Baja California north into Oregon. They stay almost entirely within dense, tangled vegetation—coastal sage scrub, thick riparian understory, and heavy brush—where they can slip quickly into cover. Because they rely on dense vegetation rather than burrows, they are harder to see and photograph, and their secretive behavior makes them appear less common than they actually are.
When comparing the two species, the combination of ear length, ear color, tail appearance, and overall coat tone provides the clearest clues. Desert cottontails look slightly taller and more open‑country in build, with long ears and a bright tail that shows when they flee. Brush rabbits look more compact, with shorter ears, a uniformly gray coat, and a tail that does not contrast strongly with the rest of the body. Habitat is often the final confirmation: a rabbit sitting in open grassland or chaparral is usually a desert cottontail, while one disappearing into a dense thicket is far more likely to be a brush rabbit.

Placental mammals are the group of terrestrial and aquatic animals whose babies develop inside the mother for a long time because they have a true placenta, which is an organ that passes food and oxygen from the mother to the embryo. This long internal development means the young are born much more fully formed than marsupials, whose babies are born very early and finish growing in a pouch, or monotremes, which lay eggs. A familiar marsupial example is the Virginia Opossum, and a common monotreme example is the Platypus. Placental mammals also lack epipubic bones, which are stiff rods in the belly region found in marsupials and monotremes. Losing those bones lets the abdomen expand during pregnancy. Their ankle has a particular locking shape called a mortise joint, which helps with stable walking and running. They usually have a strong connection between the left and right halves of the brain called the corpus callosum, which is reduced or missing in other mammal groups. And unlike monotremes, they do not have a cloaca, which is a single opening for waste and reproduction; instead, the openings are separate.

Placental mammals also lack epipubic bones, which are stiff rods in the belly region found in marsupials and monotremes. Losing those bones lets the abdomen expand during pregnancy. Their ankle has a particular locking shape called a mortise joint, which helps with stable walking and running. They usually have a strong connection between the left and right halves of the brain called the corpus callosum, which is reduced or missing in other mammal groups. And unlike monotremes, they do not have a cloaca, which is a single opening for waste and reproduction; instead, the openings are separate.

Desert Cottontails and Brush Rabbits look similar at a distance, but when you focus on their body shape, coloring, and behavior, they separate into two very different species. Desert cottontails have noticeably longer ears that end in a dark tip, and these ears stand out even when the rabbit is resting. Their fur shows warm, rusty tones along the back of the neck and on the hindlegs, giving them a slightly sun‑washed look. The tail is rounded and fluffy with a bright white edge that flashes clearly when the animal runs, which makes them easy to spot as they bound across open ground. Brush rabbits, on the other hand, have shorter ears that stay a uniform gray with no dark tip. Their coat is a cool slate‑gray without any rufous highlights, and their tail is smaller and more muted, blending into the rest of the body rather than standing out. These differences are subtle, but once you learn them, they are reliable ways to tell the two species apart.
Their habitats reflect these physical differences. Desert cottontails are widespread across the southwestern United States and northern Mexico, thriving in open or lightly vegetated areas such as desert grasslands, chaparral, pinyon‑juniper woodlands, and the edges of riparian corridors. They often rest in shallow depressions or take over abandoned burrows from other mammals, especially during the heat of the day. Brush rabbits have a much narrower range, hugging the Pacific coast from Baja California north into Oregon. They stay almost entirely within dense, tangled vegetation—coastal sage scrub, thick riparian understory, and heavy brush—where they can slip quickly into cover. Because they rely on dense vegetation rather than burrows, they are harder to see and photograph, and their secretive behavior makes them appear less common than they actually are.
When comparing the two species, the combination of ear length, ear color, tail appearance, and overall coat tone provides the clearest clues. Desert cottontails look slightly taller and more open‑country in build, with long ears and a bright tail that shows when they flee. Brush rabbits look more compact, with shorter ears, a uniformly gray coat, and a tail that does not contrast strongly with the rest of the body. Habitat is often the final confirmation: a rabbit sitting in open grassland or chaparral is usually a desert cottontail, while one disappearing into a dense thicket is far more likely to be a brush rabbit.

Their fur shows warm, rusty tones along the back of the neck and on the hindlegs, giving them a slightly sun‑washed look. The tail is rounded and fluffy with a bright white edge that flashes clearly when the animal runs, which makes them easy to spot as they bound across open ground. Brush rabbits, on the other hand, have shorter ears that stay a uniform gray with no dark tip. Their coat is a cool slate‑gray without any rufous highlights, and their tail is smaller and more muted, blending into the rest of the body rather than standing out. These differences are subtle, but once you learn them, they are reliable ways to tell the two species apart.
Their habitats reflect these physical differences. Desert cottontails are widespread across the southwestern United States and northern Mexico, thriving in open or lightly vegetated areas such as desert grasslands, chaparral, pinyon‑juniper woodlands, and the edges of riparian corridors. They often rest in shallow depressions or take over abandoned burrows from other mammals, especially during the heat of the day. Brush rabbits have a much narrower range, hugging the Pacific coast from Baja California north into Oregon. They stay almost entirely within dense, tangled vegetation—coastal sage scrub, thick riparian understory, and heavy brush—where they can slip quickly into cover. Because they rely on dense vegetation rather than burrows, they are harder to see and photograph, and their secretive behavior makes them appear less common than they actually are.
When comparing the two species, the combination of ear length, ear color, tail appearance, and overall coat tone provides the clearest clues. Desert cottontails look slightly taller and more open‑country in build, with long ears and a bright tail that shows when they flee. Brush rabbits look more compact, with shorter ears, a uniformly gray coat, and a tail that does not contrast strongly with the rest of the body. Habitat is often the final confirmation: a rabbit sitting in open grassland or chaparral is usually a desert cottontail, while one disappearing into a dense thicket is far more likely to be a brush rabbit.

"Eastern Cottontail has the widest distribution of any Sylvilagus. It is found from southern Manitoba and Quebec to Central and northwestern South America. Historically, the eastern cottontail inhabited deserts, swamps and hardwood forests, as well as rainforests and boreal forests. Currently, the eastern cottontail prefers edge environments between woody vegetation and open land. However, unlike pikas, these mammals are characterized by long, powerful hindlimbs, large ears, protruding eyes, and short, furry tails. They also have slightly curved claws and bushy soles that provide a strong grip on the ground, making them well-adapted to a cursorial (running and hopping) lifestyle. These small to moderate-sized mammals are native to all continents except Antarctica and Australia, although some species, such as the European rabbit, have been introduced to Oceania. As obligate herbivores, leporids primarily feed on grasses, herbs, clover, and other plants. The animal that I observed was a small rabbit popular in my area that varies in shades of brown with different splashes of black, white and grey on its coat. This rabbit is actually a regular in our garden during the warmer months of the summer, and can actually be held responsible for tearing and eating many of my grandma’s prized bulbed plants. This assignment allowed me to look into this particular animal that was such a common occurrence and helped me identify it as the Eastern Cottontail Rabbit or the Sylvilagus floridanus. It is in the Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata, Class Mammalia, Order Lagomorpha, and Family Lerporidae (IUCN Redlist). This rabbit species is actually the most popular in all of North America, it can be found through Canada, The US, Mexico and even parts of South America but is the most abundant in Midwestern North America (Mankin et al. 1999)

	I observed this species in a local park while walking though my neighbourhood in my home city of Markham in the York Region district, in early September as summer came to a close.  Initially an agricultural community Markham later developed into a more urbanized one after the end of World War Two, and was upgraded from town to city around five years ago (Gordon et al. 2005). Eastern Cottontails prefer habitats of grass meadows with dense growth around the edges of small shrubs and bushes, the park at which I found them was an ideal candidate (Brown et al. 1995). Due to their abundance in the region the cottontails are actually a part of the diets of many animals and have multiple predators including but not limited to domestic cats and dogs, foxes, coyotes and raccoons. The shrub or woodland habitat is essential to provide cover and shelter during both the summer and winter months (Brown et al. 1995). 

	Eastern Cottontails are herbivores and nearly exclusively depend on vegetation for their diet, this includes leaves, clovers, fruit, grass seeds, and flowers (even those from my grandma’s garden) (Chapman et al. 1972). Because these animals inhibit areas that are prone to cold, dry and snowy winters with not much greenery they tend to depend on alternate parts of plants like twigs and bark during the winter months (Chapman et al. 1972).

This species is the rabbit that you see most commonly in our region, they are around a foot long ad weight between two and five pounds. Their colour ranges from shades of brown to darker shades of grey depending on their habitat. They have long ears held erect most of the time and their namesake white fluffy tail. These rabbits usually live around three years in the wild but can last longer in captivity (Warren et al. 2015). Their breeding season usually spans from February to early September, and females reach reproductive maturity at around 3 months. Males mate with multiple females and the average is three to four litters annually, with an average number of five kits (baby rabbits) per litter (Warren et al. 2015).

According the IUCN this species is at Lower Risk or least concern with a currently sustainable increasing population (IUCN Redlist).
